conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi Ms. ___. I’m Dr. ___. I hear you came in from dialysis because of blurry vision and your blood pressure was very low in the ER. How are you feeling right now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m tired. My left eye is still blurry. And they told me my pressure was scary low.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That makes sense to be worried. In the ER your blood pressure was 58 over 38, and they gave you a small IV fluid bolus. It came up after that. Any dizziness, fainting, or chest pain now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No chest pain. I don’t feel dizzy right now, just weak.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. We’ll keep checking your pressures closely, especially around dialysis. Do you remember if you’ve been taking your midodrine at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Honestly… I haven’t been taking it like I should. I wasn’t sure it was helping.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Thanks for telling me. Midodrine helps keep your blood pressure up, especially after fluid is removed during dialysis. We’re going to restart it here and make sure you’re on a schedule you can follow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is the low pressure why I feel so wiped out?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It can be a big part of it. Your blood test called lactate was elevated when your pressure was low, which can happen when the body isn’t getting enough blood flow. After fluids, the lactate improved, which is reassuring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about my breathing? I get short of breath walking, but it’s not new.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We checked a chest X-ray today and it didn’t show pneumonia or fluid in the lungs. Since it’s not worse than usual, we’ll keep an eye on it, but nothing suggests a new lung infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Let’s talk about the vision. You said the left eye has been blurry since the venogram anesthesia during your last admission, correct?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes. I woke up and it was blurry. It hasn’t gotten worse, but it hasn’t gone away either. And my right eye is already bad from shingles.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Right. Ophthalmology examined you in the ER. They found your left eye vision improves when they use a +2.75 lens, and the inside of the eye looked normal on the dilated exam. Their impression is that this is a temporary focusing problem—loss of accommodation—after anesthesia, and it should improve over days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s not a stroke?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Based on their exam, a stroke is unlikely because the blurriness corrects with a lens and the eye exam was otherwise normal. We did think about it because you’ve had low blood pressures and you rely on the left eye, but the findings point away from a brain cause.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I live alone. I’m scared to go home like this.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s exactly why we’re admitting you—to monitor your blood pressure and make sure your vision is stable and you’re safe. We’ll also talk about supports for when you go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Any eye pain, redness, or discharge?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No pain. Just blurry.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. Any fever or chills since you left the hospital last time?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re also drawing blood cultures because of your recent MRSA bloodstream infection. So far, no signs of a new infection, and your chest X-ray is clear.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Am I still getting the vancomycin with dialysis?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. We’re continuing the plan for vancomycin given with hemodialysis to complete the full course recommended after the catheter-related MRSA bacteremia.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I also haven’t had a bowel movement in days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Thanks for mentioning that. Constipation can happen with pain meds like oxycodone and with being less active. We’ll start a bowel regimen and keep you comfortable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Overnight your blood pressure stayed low-ish but stable, and your repeat lactate came down to normal. Any dizziness when you got up?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No dizziness. Still tired. Vision is the same.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. We’ll keep midodrine twice a day. For the vision, ophthalmology expects gradual improvement. In the meantime, using over-the-counter reading glasses may help with focusing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What strength glasses?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: They found it corrected with about +2.75. Many drugstores have +2.5 or +3.0—either may help until you can get a full outpatient eye exam.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is there anything I should do to protect my good eye?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes—because you’re essentially monocular, we recommend protective eyewear: polycarbonate lenses and sunglasses when outside, and being careful with activities that could injure the eye.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re also continuing your HIV medications and your prophylaxis—Bactrim and weekly azithromycin—just as you were taking at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I noticed you changed my valacyclovir.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: In the hospital we’re using acyclovir instead of valacyclovir, but it’s the same idea—antiviral coverage. At discharge you’ll go back to your home valacyclovir.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Morning. How are the vision and energy today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Maybe a tiny bit better? Still blurry up close. My blood pressure feels okay.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s encouraging. Your pressures have been more steady since restarting midodrine. We’ll keep aiming for your dialysis dry weight—around 73.5 kilograms—so we don’t pull too much fluid.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: My throat has been sore since that procedure, and this morning it felt like food got stuck.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Thanks—given your history and immune status, that sensation can sometimes be from yeast in the esophagus. We’re going to start fluconazole: a higher loading dose today, then 100 mg daily for a total of 14 days, and we’ll see if symptoms improve.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that the same medicine I took before?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it’s the same antifungal. Let us know if swallowing becomes painful, if you can’t keep food down, or if you develop fevers.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. Also my skin itching is still bad.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see the excoriations. Your eosinophil count has been elevated before, and the Strongyloides antibody test came back negative. We’ll continue hydroxyzine as needed for itching, and we’ll arrange follow-up with Dermatology and Allergy to look for other causes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi Ms. ___. Dialysis team mentioned there was some clotting in the dialysis catheter recently and they needed a heparin dwell. Have you noticed any new pain or swelling in the left groin where the catheter is?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It’s a little tender and puffy there. I’m worried it’s infected again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s a reasonable concern given what you just went through. We examined it and don’t see drainage, but because of the swelling we ordered an ultrasound of the left groin to look for any fluid collection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your ultrasound is back: it shows no focal fluid collection along the catheter tract, which argues against an abscess.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So why is it swollen?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It may be local irritation or swelling around the line, and there’s also concern that the catheter and your known IVC narrowing can cause turbulent flow and increase the risk of clotting around the catheter. The clotting episode during dialysis is part of why we’re taking this seriously.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What can you do about that? I can’t lose this access.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. Because your access options are limited and we’re worried about thrombosis risk, we recommend starting warfarin, a blood thinner, to reduce the chance of clotting around the catheter.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Isn’t that dangerous? I’ve heard people bleed on that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Bleeding is the main risk, yes. That’s why we monitor it with a blood test called INR and adjust the dose. We’ll coordinate INR checks with your dialysis sessions so it’s closely followed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will it also help my atrial fibrillation?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It can. You’ve been in normal rhythm here, but you have a history of paroxysmal AF. In your case, anticoagulation is being started mainly for the catheter clotting concern, and it may also cover other potential reasons your cardiology team has discussed in the past.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Do I need to change what I eat?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: With warfarin, the key is consistency with foods that contain vitamin K—like leafy greens—rather than avoiding them completely. We’ll give you written instructions, and the dialysis unit will help track your INR.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. How did dialysis go today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It went okay. No big drop in pressure like before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great. Your blood pressures have been stable on midodrine. Your blood cultures have stayed negative, which is reassuring given your recent MRSA infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: My swallowing is a little better since starting the fluconazole.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good—that response supports our suspicion of candidal esophagitis. You’ll need to finish the full 14-day course even if you feel better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the vision—will it really go back to normal?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We expect continued gradual improvement. You’ve already noticed a bit of change. Use over-the-counter reading glasses for now, and it’s important you follow up with ophthalmology within a week for a full exam, especially since you rely on the left eye.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Let’s review the discharge plan. You’re going home today. Continue midodrine twice daily to prevent low blood pressure, especially around dialysis. Continue vancomycin with hemodialysis to complete the planned course. Continue your HIV medications and prophylaxis. Continue fluconazole daily to complete 14 days. And start warfarin 4 mg daily with INR checks arranged at dialysis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What should make me come back to the hospital?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Come back right away for fainting, severe dizziness, chest pain, new shortness of breath, fever or chills, worsening pain/redness/drainage at the dialysis catheter site, vomiting blood or black stools, or any sudden worsening of vision. We’ll also give you instructions about warfarin bleeding signs and your follow-up appointments.
